In all these places M has ἀδάμαντον [unconquered], which the editors corrected. In other passages of the tragedians the scribes consistently wrote ἀδάμαστος [unconquered], which Homer used. Elmsley observed (on Soph. OR. 196) that the tragedians consistently used the form ἀδάματος [unconquered].
we dwell in the city of the gods, unconquered.
to escape the beds of men, unwedded and unconquered.

Hesychius: ἄδασμον [not paying tribute]: paying no tribute, that is, not (οὐ [not] added by H. Stephanus) paying rent. Photius p. 8, 4: ἄδασμος [not paying tribute]: paying no tribute, nor apportioning tribute for the dwelling. Thus Aeschylus.

The verse is corrupt from an iambic dimeter, as will be said under ἀδελφός [brother].
and near are three winged sisters of these.
and near are these sisters of brothers.

The form ἀδελφεός [brother] was introduced by an interpolator at Sept. 576 καὶ τὸν σὸν αὖθις προσμόραν ἀδελφεόν [and again your brother, bringing doom], where Blomfield and G. Burges restored the true reading προσμολών ὁμόσπορον [having come, of the same seed]. The other example is uncertain, at line 974 πέλας δ᾽ αἵδ᾽ ἀδελφαὶ ἀδελφεῶν [and near are these sisters of brothers], since the words πέλας δ᾽ αἵδ᾽ ἀδελφαί [and near are these sisters], for which an iambic dipody is required, as the antistrophic verse 985 shows, have not yet been emended. However, it is not improbable that it should be written πέλας δ᾽ ἀδέλφ᾽ ἀδελφῶν [and near are the brothers' sisters], from which Hermann was very close when, following a different opinion about the meter, he wrote πέλας ἀδελφέ᾽ ἀδελφεῶν [near the brothers' sisters]. That in the antistrophe 985 the second dipody begins with a long syllable δίυγρα τριπάλτων πημάτων [wet with thrice-hurled woes], the same occurs at v. 1983 δορός γε τῷδ' ἀντηρέτας [rowers against this spear], although the preceding verse of Antigone is composed of pure iambs ἐπεὶ κατῆλθες ἐς πόλιν [since you came to the city]. But the particle δέ [but] is no less suitable here than in other verses of this stichomythia.
and perhaps, as I just said, signifying equal evils of brothers, as Soph. Ant. 192 said καὶ νῦν ἀδελφὰ τῶνδε κηρύξας ἔχω [and now I have proclaimed things equal to these].
brother of the one mentioned before.
